sources.news_title: KILMAR ABREGO GARCIA IS NO LONGER A 'MARYLAND MAN' — He's Self-Deporting to Spain Today
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national who entered the United States illegally roughly 15 years ago and whose case Democrats turned into a national political cause, boarded a commercial flight from the Washington, D.C. area to Madrid, Spain, on Tuesday, ABC News reported after observing him at the airport.
Multiple U.S. officials told CBS News that Abrego Garcia was expected to leave the country Tuesday on a commercial flight. ABC News reported that before clearing security, Abrego Garcia entered a Customs and Border Protection office at the airport, in part to have his ankle monitor removed — a device federal immigration officers fitted him with more than a year ago when he was returned to the United States.
The terms of his departure have not been publicly disclosed. U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has presided over his civil litigation in Maryland, issued an order Friday that remains under seal. Fox News reported that the departure followed a directive from the judge that he leave by Tuesday.
The Associated Press reported that Abrego Garcia was leaving voluntarily for Spain, which is governed by socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. According to 100PercentFedUp, his attorneys say Mexico is where he ultimately plans to go. For months, the administration and Abrego Garcia's lawyers had fought over which country would receive him — he expressed a willingness to go to Costa Rica while the administration explored Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia.
The Saga
The Trump administration deported Abrego Garcia to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison in March 2025 as part of its immigration crackdown. The administration later acknowledged the removal was an administrative error, because a 2019 immigration judge had granted him withholding of removal to that particular country.
After the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that Abrego Garcia should be returned to the United States, he was brought back last June to face human smuggling charges in Tennessee tied to a 2022 traffic stop. He pleaded not guilty, and a federal judge dismissed the indictment on vindictive-prosecution grounds. The Justice Department kept the case alive and in August the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Tennessee appealed the dismissal to the Sixth Circuit.
No member of Congress invested more political capital in the case than Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), who flew to El Salvador in April 2025 and met with Abrego Garcia personally.
"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Abrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice. I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this Administration's constant persecution."
Van Hollen also claimed the administration was "forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation."
An Instagram post indexed Tuesday showed a photo captioned as a conversation with Abrego Garcia and his wife; the post's caption was not a transcript and the account did not release its contents. It circulated as the departure reports broke.
What Was Alleged
Central to the case were allegations of Abrego Garcia's ties to MS-13, which predated his deportation by six years, according to RedState. Abrego Garcia has denied gang membership. He never received permanent legal status after entering the country illegally as a teenager. The 2019 immigration ruling protected him from removal to El Salvador — it did not grant him a right to remain in America permanently or bar the government from pursuing removal to another country.
It is not yet known whether the criminal appeal in the Sixth Circuit will continue now that he has left the country, or whether Spain's government was consulted on the sealed arrangement.
Spain's foreign ministry did not immediately comment on the arrival, according to wire reporting Tuesday.
Our Take
So ends the strangest immigration story of Trump's second term — not with a courtroom vindication for the men who spent two years insisting Kilmar Abrego Garcia was a victim of American cruelty, but with a one-way ticket to Madrid on a commercial flight he walked onto himself.
Remember what Democrats actually demanded. They demanded he be returned to the United States — and a federal judge obliged, releasing him from ICE detention onto American streets to await trial. They demanded due process, and he got it, including a dismissed indictment and an appeal still grinding through the Sixth Circuit. What they never demanded was the obvious thing: that a man in the country illegally, facing gang allegations he denies, eventually leave. Van Hollen flew to El Salvador for a photo op but could not bring himself to fly to Spain with his constituent.
The administration's March 2025 removal to El Salvador was an error — the government said so itself, and a 2019 order specifically barred sending him there. That error is why this dragged on for two years and gave the Left its martyr. But the outcome Tuesday is the correct one: Abrego Garcia is out of the United States, voluntarily, without the spectacle of a forced removal Democrats could fundraise off. He will not be in Maryland. He will not be in a Tennessee courtroom. He will be in Spain.
Patriots should mark what this cost: congressional trips, sealed orders, years of court time — all to remove a man who was removable from day one. The lesson is not that the system worked. It is that the system took two years to do what should have taken two weeks. Ask your representatives why the deportation of a single Salvadoran national required the Supreme Court, and why the answer from the Left was never "leave" — only "stay."
And notice how quiet the mainstream media will be about this self-deportation. Doesn't fit their narrative.

Kilmar Abrego García boarded a flight from the Washington, D.C., area to Madrid on Tuesday, beginning a voluntary departure from the United States after a nearly two-year legal battle that started with his mistaken deportation to a notorious Salvadoran prison.
ABC News observed Abrego García boarding the flight. The monitor had been issued after he returned to the United States. Details of the arrangement allowing him to leave remain sealed. The Associated Press reported that a person familiar with the matter said a judge had instructed him to self-deport Tuesday; The Washington Post reported that his lawyers and government attorneys negotiated the agreement.
The departure followed months of disputes over where the U.S. could send him. Abrego García had said he was willing to go to Costa Rica, while the Trump administration pursued removal to several African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia. A hearing on the government's effort to deport him to Liberia was abruptly canceled in October after Judge Paula Xinis met privately with attorneys. Sealed filings, including an order, were entered in the case last week.
Abrego García was born and raised in El Salvador, where his family ran a pupuseria. Court records say the Barrio 18 gang extorted the family and threatened to kill him and relatives. His family sent him to the United States as a teenager to live with his older brother. He later settled in Maryland with his U.S. citizen wife and children, and worked as a sheet metal apprentice.
In 2019, an immigration judge granted him "withholding of removal," ruling that he could not be sent to El Salvador because he faced a clear probability of persecution there. That protection did not give him permanent residency or prevent deportation to every country. It barred his removal to El Salvador, leaving the government able to seek another destination through immigration proceedings.
The Trump administration deported him to El Salvador on March 15, 2025, despite that order. The government later acknowledged the removal was illegal and attributed it to an "administrative error." Officials also alleged that Abrego García belonged to MS-13, a claim he denied. Public reporting traced the allegation to a 2019 Maryland police gang report based partly on a confidential informant. The Washington Post reported that the officer who prepared the report was later fired after pleading guilty to misconduct, and that the county had stopped using the field-interview form amid concerns about its reliability.
Abrego García was held at El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center, known as CECOT, as part of the Trump administration's deportation campaign. In April 2025, the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody and ensure his case was handled as it would have been had he not been improperly removed. The court did not reinstate the original deadline for his return, and directed a lower court to clarify the order. He was brought back to the United States on June 6, 2025, after federal prosecutors indicted him in Tennessee on human-smuggling charges.
Those charges stemmed from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. Abrego García pleaded not guilty. In May 2026, U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed the indictment, finding that the government had failed to rebut a presumption of vindictive prosecution. The Justice Department appealed, so the case remains subject to further court proceedings.
The public details of Abrego García's departure agreement, including what it means for his immigration proceedings, have not been disclosed. ABC News reported that he was in the process of self-deporting to Spain; his longer-term plans have not been made clear publicly.

Donald Trump’s administration has reached an agreement to let Kilmar Abrego Garcia leave the U.S. voluntarily, ending a nearly two-year legal battle over the fate of a Salvadoran immigrant whose story has been at the center of the president’s mass deportation campaign.
He boarded a commercial flight to Spain on Tuesday night.
Abrego Garcia’s case has been a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s efforts to rapidly arrest and deport tens of thousands of people from the country despite legal safeguards and humanitarian protections that the president has also eroded since returning to the White House.
The administration has spent the last year trying to deport Abrego Garcia a second time — including to Liberia — after the government unlawfully deported him to a brutal prison in his home country, triggering the high-profile legal battle for his return.
“After a protracted fight, Abrego Garcia, on his terms, boarded a flight tonight to Spain,” his legal team said in a statement Tuesday. “We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department. He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
The Independent has requested comment from the Department of Homeland Security.
Abrego Garcia, 31, has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years after fleeing gang violence in El Salvador and entering the U.S. illegally as a teenager. An immigration judge blocked the government from deporting him to his home country in 2019.
But last year, federal agents abruptly deported Abrego Garcia to El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison where he says he endured torture and “severe” abuse for several weeks before he was transferred to a separate jail.
Government officials admitted in court that his removal was due to an “error,” and several federal judges and a unanimous Supreme Court ordered the administration to “facilitate” his return.
The government spent weeks battling those orders while White House officials launched a barrage of public attacks against him and declared that he would never again step foot in the country.
He was returned to the U.S. last June — only to face allegations that he illegally moved other immigrants across the country. He pleaded not guilty.
A federal judge later dismissed the criminal case against him after finding that the administration unlawfully targeted him as part of a smear campaign.
“Objective evidence” has shown that federal prosecutors only brought charges against Abrego Garcia after he won his lawsuit challenging his arrest and removal, the judge ruled.
The administration has, at the same time, tried to deport him to at least five different countries, including four in Africa, and refused to let him leave the country for Costa Rica.
In a memo issued in March, ICE’s then-acting director Todd Lyons argued that sending him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”
In April, the administration “analyzed and eliminated all other options” from the table and settled on Liberia as “a final country of removal,” despite his own attempts to voluntarily remove himself to Costa Rica.
Government lawyers argued in court documents that the U.S. has expended significant political capital and entered “high-stakes” and “extensive negotiations” to send him to Liberia.
But the judge overseeing his deportation case had blocked Immigration and Customs Enforcement from re-deporting or detaining him, noting earlier this year that the government has made “one empty threat after another to remove him to countries in Africa with no real chance of success.”
Both sides were scheduled to discuss his case at a hearing in October, but U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis abruptly ended the hearing after she met privately with attorneys in her chambers.
Judge Xinis issued an order in the case on November 20 but it remains sealed.
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who traveled to El Salvador in an attempt to secure Abrego Garcia’s release from prisons there, said his constituent is now “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”
“While the Trump administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said in a statement Tuesday night.
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution,” he added. “This is a victory for due process and our Constitution.”

sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaving U.S. today, heading to Spain
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year and sent to a notorious prison in his home country, is planning to leave the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.
CBS News was first to report Abrego Garcia's plans earlier Tuesday.
Abrego Garcia, whose case became an early flashpoint in the debate over the Trump administration's deportation crackdown, is set to fly to Spain on a commercial flight Tuesday, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter, who requested anonymity to talk about an arrangement that has not been disclosed publicly.
The exact nature of his arrangements and the conditions of his departure from the U.S. were not immediately clear. But the federal judge in Maryland overseeing his civil legal case issued an order Friday that remains sealed.
"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said. He reiterated the Trump administration's allegation that Abrego Garcia belongs to a gang — which his legal team has denied — and said he now "cannot terrorize innocent Americans."
CBS News has reached out to an attorney and representatives for Abrego Garcia.
The move by Abrego Garcia comes after the Trump administration spent months trying to deport the man, who came to the U.S. illegally 15 years ago and had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when he was detained by immigration authorities in March 2025. He was then deported to El Salvador and held for months in the country's CECOT prison, despite a previous court order barring him from being sent back to his home country. He was brought back to the United States last year to face criminal charges.
Abrego Garcia has maintained for more than a year that if he had to leave the U.S. again, he would be willing to go to Costa Rica, and designated the Central American nation as his preferred country of removal.
But the Trump administration had resisted that suggestion and instead unsuccessfully sought to deport Abrego Garcia to numerous African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana. In more recent months, the Department of Homeland Security said it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia — part of a broader practice of sending deportees to countries in Africa.
Abrego Garcia's departure from the U.S. came weeks after a hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has been presiding over a civil case stemming from his deportation last year, was abruptly cancelled. The judge ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year to release Abrego Garcia from immigration custody and has continued to bar immigration authorities from detaining him while litigation continued.
But the Trump administration had sought to lift Xinis' orders, which it said were the only impediments to Abrego Garcia's "prompt removal." The Justice Department said in March that the government was "ready, willing, and able" to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia in West Africa.
Abrego Garcia's case gained national prominence last year after a top administration official acknowledged that his removal to El Salvador was an "error." Following his arrest by immigration authorities in March 2025, Abrego Garcia was among the more than 200 immigrants who were sent to El Salvador and detained at its notorious supermax prison, the Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT.
But Abrego Garcia had been granted a withholding of removal by an immigration judge in 2019, which prevented immigration authorities from deporting him to his home country of El Salvador because he was at risk of persecution by local gangs.
In April 2025, Xinis ordered the Department of Homeland Security to bring Abrego Garcia back to the U.S., and the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.
The Trump administration ultimately brought Abrego Garcia back to the U.S. in June 2025, but only after he was indicted on federal charges of human smuggling stemming from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. Abrego Garcia pleaded not guilty and in May, a federal judge in Tennessee dismissed the criminal charges on the grounds that his prosecution was vindictive.
The Justice Department has appealed that decision, and arguments before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit are scheduled for February.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation became a flashpoint in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, left the United States for Spain on Tuesday under an agreement to depart voluntarily.
Reporters saw Abrego Garcia board a flight from a Washington-area airport to Madrid, ABC News reported. Before going through security, he stopped at a Customs and Border Protection office, in part to have his ankle monitor removed, a source told the network.
One of his attorneys, Sean Hecker, told The Washington Post that Abrego Garcia was leaving for Spain Tuesday evening. Two people briefed on the case described a negotiated agreement for the 31-year-old to depart voluntarily.
The terms have not been made public. U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who oversees his civil case in Maryland, issued an order Friday that remains sealed, CBS News reported. The judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport on Tuesday, the Associated Press reported.
Abrego Garcia entered the U.S. illegally as a teenager and settled in Maryland, where he has an American wife and child. In 2019, an immigration judge barred his removal to El Salvador because a gang had threatened his family.
Immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 and sent him to El Salvador’s CECOT prison anyway, which an official later called an “administrative error.” The administration has said he is a member of MS-13, which he denies, according to ABC News.
After the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release, he was returned in June 2025, but only after a Tennessee grand jury indicted him on human smuggling charges stemming from a 2022 traffic stop. He pleaded not guilty.
A federal judge dismissed those charges in May, finding the prosecution was vindictive. The Justice Department has appealed, and arguments before the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals are set for February, according to CBS News.
Spain, Not Liberia
The administration spent months trying to send Abrego Garcia to a third country, naming Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and most recently Liberia, the Associated Press reported. He had asked to go to Costa Rica, which had agreed to take him.
Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, wrote in a March memo that sending him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States,” according to the AP.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who traveled to El Salvador to meet Abrego Garcia after his deportation, said in a statement that the administration was “forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him.”

After the U.S. State Department obtained diplomatic assurances from Costa Rica as part of the abortive plea deal negotiations, Abrego Garcia identified the nation as his preferred destination, despite also claiming he feared persecution or torture upon his arrival.
While Abrego Garcia will reportedly self-deport to Spain, The Times reported that his legal team indicated he intends to eventually settle in Mexico.
Abrego Garcia sued the Trump administration after he was deported to El Salvador, which courts have determined violated a 2019 final deportation order that contained a withholding of removal provision stating he was forbidden from being sent to Guatemala. Judges have since determined the withholding-of-removal order actually referred to El Salvador.
Following the March 2025 deportation to El Salvador, the Trump administration initially said it had no mechanism to force President Nayib Bukele to surrender return a citizen of El Salvador to the United States.
Abrego Garcia was only returned to the country after a grand jury returned an indictment accusing him of participating in a human smuggling conspiracy, which followed April 2025 reporting by The Tennessee Star of his November 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee.
During the traffic stop, Abrego Garcia was revealed to be driving without a valid license and transporting nine individuals who lacked identification and did not speak English. The Star was the first to confirm with the Tennessee Highway Patrol (THP) that troopers were instructed to release Abrego Garcia by the “Biden-era FBI.”
Prosecutors later confirmed that an agent with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) reviewed The Star’s reporting and forwarded her findings to the federal prosecutor for the Middle District of Tennessee, ultimately leading to the charges against Abrego Garcia.
The criminal case against Abrego Garcia was dismissed earlier this year by U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama. He dismissed the case, claiming the DOJ did not defeat the presumption that the administration was vindictively prosecuting Abrego Garcia.
The Trump administration has appealed, and earlier this month, the DOJ submitted a brief to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals urging the appellate court to reverse Crenshaw’s decision, arguing the judge was wrong to consider potential vindictiveness so early in the case.
Last year, The Star received the Dao Prize for Best Local Journalism for its reporting on Abrego Garcia.

The move by Abrego Garcia comes after the Trump administration spent months trying to deport the man, who came to the U.S. illegally 15 years ago and had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when he was detained by immigration authorities in March 2025. He was then deported to El Salvador and held for months in the country’s CECOT prison, despite a previous court order barring him from being sent back to his home country. He was brought back to the United States last year to face criminal charges.
Abrego Garcia has maintained for more than a year that if he had to leave the U.S. again, he would be willing to go to Costa Rica, and designated the Central American nation as his preferred country of removal.
But the Trump administration had resisted that suggestion and instead unsuccessfully sought to deport Abrego Garcia to numerous African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana. In more recent months, the Department of Homeland Security said it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia — part of a broader practice of sending deportees to countries in Africa.
Abrego Garcia’s departure from the U.S. came weeks after a hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has been presiding over a civil case stemming from his deportation last year, was abruptly cancelled. The judge ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year to release Abrego Garcia from immigration custody and has continued to bar immigration authorities from detaining him while litigation continued.
But the Trump administration had sought to lift Xinis’ orders, which it said were the only impediments to Abrego Garcia’s “prompt removal.” The Justice Department said in March that the government was “ready, willing, and able” to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia in West Africa.
Abrego Garcia’s case gained national prominence last year after a top administration official acknowledged that his removal to El Salvador was an “error.” Following his arrest by immigration authorities in March 2025, Abrego Garcia was among the more than 200 immigrants who were sent to El Salvador and detained at its notorious supermax prison, the Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT.
But Abrego Garcia had been granted a withholding of removal by an immigration judge in 2019, which prevented immigration authorities from deporting him to his home country of El Salvador because he was at risk of persecution by local gangs.
In April 2025, Xinis ordered the Department of Homeland Security to bring Abrego Garcia back to the U.S., and the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.
The Trump administration ultimately brought Abrego Garcia back to the U.S. in June 2025, but only after he was indicted on federal charges of human smuggling stemming from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee.
